setup: IFRS 9 lifetime ECL on a \$50m two-year loan book. Expected loss (PD × EAD × LR) is \$2.10m in year 1 and \$1.33m in year 2. The effective interest rate is 7.9%. Defaults are assumed to occur in the middle of each year, so the losses are discounted for 0.5 and 1.5 years.
ask: Compared with discounting the two losses for a full 1 and 2 years, the mid-year convention gives a present value that is:

options.label: Lower
options.why: Read mid-year as a longer wait. Half a year of discounting is less than a full year, so each loss is discounted less and the PV is higher.

options.label: The same
options.why: The rate and the cash flows are unchanged, but the discount periods are not: 0.5 and 1.5 years instead of 1 and 2, so the PV differs.

takeaway: Mid-year default means shorter discount periods, so a higher PV of expected loss than the end-of-year convention.

reading: CR-5: Introduction to Credit Risk Modeling and Assessment
setup: Standardised approach. Bank M holds Tier 1 capital of \$60m and Tier 2 capital of \$20m. Its assets are \$400m of corporate loans (risk weight 100%), \$300m of residential mortgages (50%) and \$200m of loans to highly rated banks (20%), \$900m in total. The unweighted ratio of capital to total assets is 8.9%.
ask: Bank M's capital adequacy ratio (capital / RWA) is:

options.label: Below 8.9%
options.why: Assumed risk weighting inflates the denominator. Weights of 100% or less can only shrink RWA below total assets, so the ratio rises.

options.label: Equal to 8.9%
options.why: That needs every asset at a 100% weight. Here half the book is weighted at 50% or 20%.

takeaway: Risk weights below 100% shrink the denominator, so CAR sits above the simple capital-to-assets ratio.

reading: CR-5: Introduction to Credit Risk Modeling and Assessment
setup: A bank has \$120m of total capital and \$1,000m of RWA (CAR 12%). \$200m of its exposures carry a 100% risk weight. The regulator raises that weight to 150%; capital and exposures are unchanged.
ask: Total RWA after the change is closest to:

options.label: \$1,200m
options.why: Added the whole \$200m exposure again instead of only the extra 50% of it.

options.label: \$1,300m
options.why: Added the new \$300m of weighted exposure without removing the old \$200m.

options.label: \$1,500m
options.why: Multiplied all RWA by 1.5, although only the \$200m class is re-weighted.

takeaway: Swap the old weighted amount for the new one; do not stack one on top of the other. CAR falls to about 10.9%.

reading: CR-5: Introduction to Credit Risk Modeling and Assessment
setup: Basel II IRB retail book. $EAD = \$400$m, $LGD = 35\%$, worst-case default rate $WCDR = 10\%$, $PD = 2\%$, maturity adjustment $MA = 1$. $RWA = 12.5 \times EAD \times LGD \times (WCDR - PD) \times MA$.
ask: RWA is closest to:

options.label: ≈ \$11m
options.why: Left out the 12.5 multiplier (the reciprocal of the 8% capital ratio), so this is the capital charge $K \times EAD$, not RWA.

options.label: ≈ \$400m
options.why: Left out LGD: $12.5 \times 400 \times 0.08$.

options.label: ≈ \$1,750m
options.why: Left out the $(WCDR - PD)$ term altogether: $12.5 \times 400 \times 0.35$.

takeaway: Check the order of magnitude: capital charge of about 3% of EAD, times 12.5, gives RWA of about 35% of EAD.

reading: CR-7: Credit Scoring and Retail Credit Risk Management
setup: CAP accuracy ratio: $AR = \dfrac{\text{area between model curve and random line}}{\text{area between perfect and random line}}$. The area between the perfect line and the random line is 0.40. Provider A's curve encloses 0.34 above the random line.
ask: Provider A's accuracy ratio is closest to:

options.why: Multiplied the two areas ($0.34 \times 0.40$) instead of dividing.
Reported the raw area and never divided by the perfect-model area.
Inverted the ratio ($0.40/0.34$). A model cannot do better than perfect, so AR cannot exceed 1.

takeaway: AR is the share of the perfect model's lift that the model captures, so it lies between 0 and 1.

reading: CR-7: Credit Scoring and Retail Credit Risk Management
setup: A bank has 10,000 loans of \$10,000 each, all priced at a flat 10%, LGD 50%. Prime: 6,000 loans, PD 1%. Subprime: 4,000 loans, PD 6%. A competitor offers prime borrowers 8%, so half the prime customers leave under flat pricing; subprime customers stay.
ask: Under flat pricing, annual risk-adjusted income (interest less expected loss) from the prime customers who remain is closest to:

options.label: \$5.70m
options.why: Counted all 6,000 prime loans, although half have left.

options.label: \$3.00m
options.why: Took interest only on the 3,000 remaining loans and left out expected loss.

options.label: \$0.15m
options.why: Took only the expected loss on the 3,000 remaining loans instead of interest minus expected loss.

takeaway: Reprice only after you count who is left: lost customers take their income with them.

setup: A protection buyer pays a CDS spread of 90 bp a year on a \$100m, 5-year CDS, in quarterly instalments in arrears. A credit event occurs exactly one month after the most recent payment date.
ask: The accrued premium the buyer must still pay at the credit event is closest to:

options.why: Used the full annual premium.
Paid a full quarter, ignoring that only one month has accrued.
Counted the two months left in the quarter instead of the one month already elapsed.

takeaway: On a credit event the buyer pays only the premium accrued since the last payment date, then payments stop.

setup: You sell \$1m of protection on each of the 125 names in a 5-year CDX NA IG index quoted 141 / 143 bp. At the start of year 3, before the annual premium is paid, one name defaults. You pay the full \$1m notional on it (ignore the bond you receive). The year-3 premium is paid on the other 124 names.
ask: Your net cash flow for year 3 is:

options.label: A net outflow
options.why: Counted the \$1m payout and forgot that the premium on the 124 survivors is about \$1.75m.

takeaway: A protection seller collects the bid spread on the survivors; one default of 125 costs less than the year's premium.

setup: A Ba-rated bond has an unconditional probability of default in year 3 of 1.914%. The probability of surviving through the end of year 2 is 97.413%.
ask: The probability of default in year 3, conditional on no earlier default, compared with 1.914% is:

options.label: Lower
options.why: Multiplied by survival ($1.914\% \times 0.974 = 1.865\%$). Conditioning on survival divides by it.

options.label: Equal
options.why: Treated conditional and unconditional probabilities as the same thing. They differ whenever survival to the start of the period is below 100%.

takeaway: Conditional PD = unconditional PD ÷ survival to the start of the period, so it is always the larger of the two.

setup: A 2-year corporate bond yields 190 bp over the risk-free rate. The recovery rate is 35%. Use the approximation: average hazard rate $\approx$ spread / (1 − recovery).
ask: The average hazard rate is closest to:

options.label: ≈ 0.29% a year
options.why: Read 190 bp as 0.19% instead of 1.90%, then divided by LGD.

options.label: ≈ 0.95% a year
options.why: Divided the spread by the 2-year maturity and never applied LGD.

options.label: ≈ 29% a year
options.why: Read 190 bp as 19% instead of 1.90%, then divided by LGD.

takeaway: Hazard rate is spread divided by LGD, so it is a bit above the spread. A hazard rate below the spread means a slip.

setup: Single-period bond. Risk-free rate $r = 2.0\%$, default probability 3.0%, loss given default 60% (recovery $R = 40\%$). The minimum spread $z$ solves $(1-PD)(1+r+z) + PD \times R = 1 + r$.
ask: The minimum spread $z$ compared with the rule of thumb $PD \times LGD = 1.80\%$ is:

options.label: Below 1.80%
options.why: Assumed the rule of thumb is an upper bound. The exact $z$ is larger: $z = PD(1+r-R)/(1-PD)$ divides by survival and includes the time value on the lost principal.

options.label: Equal to 1.80%
options.why: Used $z = PD \times LGD$ as exact. It drops the factor $1/(1-PD)$ and the $r$ in $(1 + r - R)$.

takeaway: z is slightly above PD × LGD, because the survivors must also cover the time value of the money lost.

setup: A GBP 85m retail exposure. One-year average PD 2.50%, recovery rate 72%. A one-factor Gaussian copula gives a 99.9% worst-case default rate of 10.73% (1-year). Credit VaR $= L \times (1 - RR) \times V$.
ask: The 99.9% credit VaR is closest to:

options.label: ≈ GBP 0.6m
options.why: Used the average PD of 2.5% instead of the 99.9% worst-case default rate.

options.label: ≈ GBP 9.1m
options.why: Left out the loss given default ($1 - RR$): $85 \times 10.73\%$.

options.label: ≈ GBP 24m
options.why: Assumed the whole book defaults and applied only LGD: $85 \times 28\%$.

takeaway: Credit VaR = exposure × LGD × worst-case default rate. Three factors, each well below 1.

setup: Modus Corp has a 7-year, 5% coupon bond rated AA. The 7-year CDS spread is 3%. Swap fixed rates are 3% for 5 years and 4% for 7 years. To rule out arbitrage the bond's yield spread over the matching swap rate must equal the CDS spread.
ask: Which swap rate is the benchmark for Modus's bond yield?

options.label: 3% (5-year swap rate)
options.why: Matched the wrong maturity. The bond is a 7-year bond, so the 7-year swap rate applies.

options.label: 5% (the bond coupon)
options.why: Confused the coupon with a market benchmark. The coupon says nothing about the swap curve.

takeaway: Match the benchmark swap rate to the bond's maturity; then yield = swap rate + CDS spread.

setup: A 5-year CDS reference entity has a constant hazard rate of 1.5% a year (continuous), so survival to the end of year $t$ is $e^{-0.015t}$. Notional \$10m, recovery 40%.
ask: The unconditional probability that default happens during year 3 is closest to:

options.why: Took the cumulative default probability to the end of year 3, $1 - e^{-0.045}$, which includes years 1 and 2.
Used the hazard rate itself. That is the default probability conditional on surviving to the start of the year; the unconditional figure is smaller.
Reported the survival probability to the end of year 3 instead of a default probability.

takeaway: Unconditional year-3 PD is the drop in survival over that year: below the hazard rate, because some names have already gone.

setup: Your firm sells a European call on Electric Inc. (stock \$47, strike \$25, 3 months, implied volatility 23%) and receives the premium in full upfront. The risk-free rate is 1.5%.
ask: Your counterparty credit exposure to the buyer is:

options.label: About \$22, the option's intrinsic value
options.why: Treated the option's value as money the buyer owes. The buyer owes nothing more; you are the one who may owe a payoff.

options.label: About \$47, the stock price
options.why: Used the underlying's price. Exposure is a claim on the counterparty, and a written option gives you no claim.

working.label: Premium
working.display: Received in full at inception, so the buyer owes nothing further

working.label: Value to you
working.display: A written option can never be worth more than nothing to you, so exposure $= \max(V, \text{nothing})$ is nil

takeaway: Credit exposure is a claim on the counterparty. An option seller who has been paid upfront has none.

setup: An investor has agreed to pay \$2.6m and receive €2m at a future date (rate 1.30 USD/EUR). Before settlement the euro rises to 1.35 USD/EUR, and the counterparty defaults before settlement. Ignore collateral and recovery.
ask: At the default, the investor's contract is:

options.label: Out of the money, so there is no loss
options.why: Wrong direction. The investor receives euros, and euros are now worth more than the \$2.6m owed.

options.label: In the money, so the investor loses the replacement cost
Worth zero, so the investor loses the full \$2.6m
options.why: That is settlement risk, which needs the dollars to be paid and the euros not delivered. Before settlement the loss is only the replacement cost.

takeaway: Pre-settlement loss is the positive replacement cost, not the notional. Receiving the currency that has risen means the position is in the money.

setup: Prime Bank receives 8% fixed on a GBP 200m, 5-year annual-pay swap. After one year, four payments remain and the market swap rate has fallen 150 bp to 6.5%. The mark-to-market is the 1.5% annual advantage on GBP 200m times the annuity factor for the remaining payments, discounted at 6.5%.
ask: The annuity factor for four annual payments at 6.5% is closest to:

options.why: Counted the original five payments instead of the four that remain.
Added up four payments with no discounting.

takeaway: An annuity factor is below the number of payments, here 3.4 against 4. The swap is in the money to Prime Bank, so exposure is positive.

setup: A market maker holds a fixed-for-floating swap with \$80.0m notional. Its replacement cost is 3.0% of notional, \$2.4m. The counterparty's one-year default probability is 1.0% and recovery is 40% of the claim.
ask: The expected one-year credit loss on the current exposure is closest to:

options.label: ≈ \$480k
options.why: Applied PD and LGD to the \$80m notional instead of the \$2.4m replacement cost.

options.label: ≈ \$1.4m
options.why: Left out the default probability: exposure × LGD.

options.label: ≈ \$48m
options.why: Left out both the default probability and the replacement-cost step: notional × LGD.

takeaway: Expected loss = exposure × PD × LGD. The exposure is the replacement cost, not the notional.

setup: A hedge fund's positions with AB&B, all under an enforceable netting agreement (positive means AB&B owes the fund), in USD m: A +44.0, B +88.0, C −35.2, D −3.3, E +20.0. AB&B defaults with zero recovery.
ask: The fund's exposure after netting compared with the largest single contract, B at +88.0, is:

options.label: Below 88.0
options.why: Assumed netting always cuts exposure below the biggest claim. The other positives (A and E, 64.0) outweigh the negatives (38.5), so the net is more than B alone.

takeaway: Netting sums the whole book first, then floors at zero. The negatives only offset 38.5 of the 152.0 owed.

setup: An uncollateralised derivative has a base value of +\$50.0m. xVA terms (each stated positive): CVA \$5.0m cost, DVA \$2.0m benefit, FVA \$1.0m cost, ColVA 0, KVA \$4.0m cost, MVA \$3.0m cost.
ask: The net xVA adjustment to the \$50.0m is closest to:

options.label: −\$15.0m
options.why: Treated DVA as a cost as well: $5 + 1 + 4 + 3 + 2 = 15$. Own default risk is a benefit to the firm.

options.label: −\$13.0m
options.why: Ignored DVA, counting costs only.

options.label: −\$3.0m
options.why: Counted only CVA and DVA ($-5 + 2$) and left out FVA, KVA and MVA.

takeaway: Costs (CVA, FVA, KVA, MVA) reduce value; DVA is the one benefit. Sign each term before adding.

setup: A CCP's loss waterfall, in order: defaulter's margin \$80m, defaulter's default-fund contribution \$30m, CCP's own capital \$25m, surviving members' default-fund contributions \$200m, then assessment calls up to \$700m. A clearing member defaults and the loss is \$275m.
ask: Will the CCP have to make assessment calls?

options.label: Yes, the default fund is exhausted first
options.why: Left out the surviving members' \$200m, so only \$135m seemed available. The \$275m loss reaches into the default fund but does not exhaust it.

takeaway: Walk the waterfall in order: defaulter pays first, CCP capital next, survivors' fund after that. Assessment is the last resort.

setup: A CCP's waterfall: defaulter's margin \$80m, defaulter's default-fund contribution \$30m, CCP's own capital \$25m, surviving members' default fund \$200m, then assessment calls. A member defaults with a total loss of \$420m.
ask: After the defaulter's margin and contribution and the CCP's own capital are used, but before the surviving members' fund, the unmet loss is closest to:

options.label: \$340m
options.why: Applied only the defaulter's margin ($420 - 80$).

options.label: \$310m
options.why: Applied the defaulter's margin and contribution but skipped the CCP's own capital.

options.label: \$85m
options.why: Went one layer too far: that is the loss left after the surviving members' \$200m as well.

takeaway: Each layer is applied in order. Here \$285m still needs the survivors' fund, which then leaves \$85m for assessment calls.
